title: What My Father Taught Me About Learning Slowly
script: Narrator: [reflective] My father never finished secondary school. He started working at fourteen, and books were never really part of his life.
Narrator: When I was young, I sometimes felt embarrassed that he couldn't help me with my homework the way other fathers could.
Narrator: But at fifty, something surprising happened. My father decided to learn how to read English, slowly, using an old phrasebook.
Narrator: [surprised] Every evening after dinner, he sat at the table with that small book, moving his finger slowly under each line.
Narrator: At first, I thought it was a strange hobby for a man his age, something that would not last more than a week.
Narrator: [patiently] Months passed, and he kept going, one page some nights, sometimes just a few words on tired nights.
Narrator: I asked him once why he was doing this so late in life. He said, learning late is still learning, my son.
Narrator: He told me he simply wanted to read the labels on medicine bottles without asking anyone for help.
Narrator: [warmly] That small, humble goal stayed with me. He was not trying to become fluent, just a little more capable.
Narrator: Watching him struggle patiently with simple words taught me something my own classes never had.
Narrator: I used to give up quickly when something felt hard, closing the book after only a few frustrating minutes.
Narrator: [determined] Now, when I study something difficult, I think of my father's finger moving slowly under those English words.
Narrator: I remind myself that slow progress is still progress, and starting late is still better than never starting.
Narrator: My father can now read simple instructions on his own, something that once felt impossible for him before.
Narrator: He is not fluent, and he never wanted to be. He just wanted to understand a little more than yesterday.
Narrator: [proud] That, I think, is a quiet and honest kind of education, the kind nobody grades but changes you completely.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's father do at fourteen?
options: He started working, and books were never part of his life
quiz.explanation: The father started working at fourteen, and books were never really part of his life.

quiz.question: What did the father decide to learn at fifty?
options: How to read English using an old phrasebook
quiz.explanation: At fifty, the father decided to learn how to read English, using an old phrasebook.

quiz.question: Why did the father want to learn English?
options: To read the labels on medicine bottles without help
quiz.explanation: He told his son he simply wanted to read medicine labels without asking anyone for help.

quiz.question: What lesson did the narrator take from watching his father?
options: Only young people can learn well
quiz.explanation: The narrator reminds himself that slow progress is still progress, and starting late beats never starting.

quiz.question: What can the father do now?
options: Read simple instructions on his own
quiz.explanation: The father can now read simple instructions on his own, though he is not fluent.

quiz.question: How did the father study each evening?
options: He followed each line with his finger
He listened to a university class
He asked his son to read everything
quiz.explanation: He used a slow physical method with the phrasebook.

quiz.question: What does “fluent” mean here?
options: Able to use the language easily
quiz.explanation: The father does not aim for easy use of all English.

quiz.question: Why was the medicine-label goal important?
options: He wanted to become a doctor
quiz.explanation: Reading labels himself would reduce his need to ask others.

quiz.question: What changed in the narrator’s study habits?
options: He continued longer when work felt hard
quiz.explanation: Watching his father made slow progress feel valuable.

quiz.question: What is the main contrast in the story?
options: Fast learning is better than slow learning
School grades matter more than daily skills
A small goal creates a big personal change
quiz.explanation: The father seeks only simple reading, but the effort inspires his son deeply.
